name: Freya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the HR admin team at a big food manufacturer, we make frozen ready meals, lasagne, curries, pies. Six of us handle contracts, new starters, sick notes and right-to-work checks for about two thousand factory staff. A normal day is new-starter paperwork in the morning, a disciplinary meeting I take notes in, and an afternoon of answering line managers who want someone hired yesterday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the new starters, honestly. On a Monday morning I walk the new line operatives round the factory and you can see who's nervous and who's going to be great. What wears me out is the forms, and being a junior manager who still has to ask my boss about half the decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was a lot of fuss. I'd say it at Sunday lunch with my family, where everyone has opinions. At work I'd say it's fine to use what helps and ignore the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady work. The factory always needs people, the HR team stays at six, and I keep learning to manage. I live near my parents, rent's cheap, and I've got about four months saved, so I feel all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, sign up for the HR qualification the company pays for, and keep using the AI now and then for drafting letters. I'd save a bit more, maybe 200 a month, because I want to buy a small house in town eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at Sunday lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother would say AI is the future, and my dad would say people always need bread and ready meals. My dad says people will always need someone to cook the lasagne, and in this picture he wins the argument. I'd side with Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The factory had a bad year two years ago when a supermarket contract went. That's always in the back of your mind. But the order book's good now.

say: I always thought AI was **a lot of fuss**, I'd say at Sunday lunch.
At work I'd say use what helps and **ignore the rest**.
think: The factory **always needs people**, and the HR team stays at six.
Cheap rent and **four months saved** make me feel all right.
do: Sign up for the **HR qualification** the company pays for.
Keep using AI now and then for **drafting letters**.
Save about **200 a month** towards a small house.
feel: **Calm** and content, with family and cheap rent close by.
S0.quote: My dad says people will always need someone to cook the lasagne, and in this picture he wins the argument.
fieldNote: She feels **secure**: cheap rent, steady factory, family nearby.
Her only background worry is a lost **supermarket contract** two years ago.
Her views are shaped by **family conversation**.

steps.text: Save 200 a month towards a small house
Draft standard HR letters with the AI assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after the people who lose out, through work and training, not handouts. I'd say it at church and to my family. At work I'd be sensible and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, HR admin is exactly what goes first. Contracts, checks, letters, booking inductions, a system does all that. If the six of us become two, I'm junior, so I might not be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, so I'm useful when they come in. I'd ask to move toward the training side, running inductions on the factory floor, because that's people and places. And I'd save harder, maybe 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not dramatic about it, but I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marlene, who's been doing contracts for twenty years and is brilliant at spotting mistakes. A system that checks contracts will make my colleague Marlene's twenty years of spotting mistakes look like nothing. I'd try to get her into the training side with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why training rather than staying in HR?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because training means standing on the factory floor in a hairnet, showing people how to work safely. That's harder for a computer. And I like it more.

say: Look after people through **work and training**, not handouts.
I'd say it **at church** and stay sensible and practical at work.
think: **HR admin** is exactly what goes first: contracts, checks and letters.
If six become two, I'm **junior** and might not stay.
do: Use AI tools more so I'm **useful** when they come in.
feel: **Anxious**, not dramatic, but she can **see it coming**.
S1.quote: A system that checks contracts will make my colleague Marlene's twenty years of spotting mistakes look like nothing.
fieldNote: She sees **HR admin** as squarely exposed.
Her plan is to move into **factory training**, where people and places matter.
She favours **work and training** over handouts.

steps.text: Use the AI tools daily for contracts and letters
Apply to run inductions in factory-floor training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families should come first. I'd say it at church and at Sunday lunch. At work I'd keep calm for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone within the first year. HR paperwork is thinking work, and if a machine can do it, the company won't pay six people. The factory floor lasts until about 2031, so if I'm in training or on the line, I get three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into factory training as fast as possible, even if it's less pay. I'd stop saving for the house and keep the money as a cushion. I'd lean on my parents, maybe move back in to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed, not the change itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say come home. My mum would have my old room ready before I'd even finished telling her about the job. I'd hate it a bit, but I'd be grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the factory floor job be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, only until the robots come. But three years is something. And I'd rather be useful than sitting at home.

I'd say it **at church** and keep calm at work for the team.
think: My **HR job goes** within the first year.
The **factory floor** gives three more years until about 2031.
do: Move into **factory training** fast, even for less pay.
Stop house saving and keep a **cash cushion**.
**Move back in** with my parents to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by the speed, not the change itself.
S2.quote: My mum would have my old room ready before I'd even finished telling her about the job.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly, because HR paperwork is thinking work.
Her parents are a **ready safety net**, offering her old room straight away.
She values **being useful** over being comfortable.

steps.text: Transfer into factory-floor training even at lower pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's plan sensibly and not panic. I'd say it at work. At church I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep HR for three or four years. By 2031 the paperwork's gone, and I'd want to be on the factory side before then. That's enough time to get a proper qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time training qualification in the first year, to run inductions and safety training. I'd keep saving, maybe even buy a small house before it hits. I'd tell my team to start thinking too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house if the job might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small house in town costs less than renting for long. I'd rather own a two-bed terrace near my parents than pay rent to someone else when the work runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To start learning something on the side. I'd tell them about the training route. I'd be honest.

say: We have **five years**, so plan sensibly and don't panic.
At church I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: I'd keep HR for **three or four years**, until 2031.
That's enough time to get a **proper qualification**.
do: Start a **part-time training qualification** in the first year.
Keep saving, maybe **buy a small house** before it hits.
Tell my team to start **thinking ahead**.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a two-bed terrace near my parents than pay rent to someone else when the work runs out.
fieldNote: She would move to the **factory side** before 2031.
She thinks owning a **cheap house** is safer than renting.
She plans to be **honest** with her team.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time workplace training qualification
Buy a two-bed terrace near her parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to plan, if people are sensible. I'd say it at church and at work. I'd sound fairly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could stay in HR for a while, get my qualification, then move into training. Hands-on work lasts until about 2039. I'd be forty, and I'd have had a good career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep HR for now and do the training qualification over a couple of years. I'd buy the house. I'd maybe think about settling down and having a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quiet. It's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten years of warning is enough time to meet someone, get married and still raise children before the robots come. My faith says you don't stop living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person starting at the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade as well as an office skill. An apprenticeship on the engineering side would last longer than an HR job. Hands and head.

I'd say it at church and at work, sounding **fairly relaxed**.
think: I could stay in HR, **get qualified**, then move into training.
Hands-on work lasts until **about 2039**, giving a good career.
do: Keep HR and do the **training qualification** over two years.
Think about **settling down** and having a family.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is enough time to meet someone, get married and still raise children before the robots come.
fieldNote: Her faith shapes a **don't stop living** attitude.
She recommends **apprenticeships** to young people over office skills.
Ten years lets her plan **family** and career together.

steps.text: Complete a training qualification over two years
Buy a small house near her parents
Make room to settle down and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose my job before I could get properly into training. What would help is my family, and a company that offers people apprenticeships and real training, not just a payout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith and family, which matter more than people think. When work gets shaky, a family that has your old room ready matters more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: When work gets shaky, a family that has your old room ready matters more than any government scheme.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old HR lead** of six at a frozen-food manufacturer.
She uses **AI now and then**, lives near her parents and goes to church.
She is **calm** in the plateau, with cheap rent and about four months saved.
She sees **HR admin** as squarely exposed, so her plan is factory-floor training.
Her **family** is her safety net in every scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job before moving into training.
whatWouldHelp: A company that offers **apprenticeships** and real training.
